c.tagline: Desert gateway to the Kaluts, built around a magnificent Safavid bazaar.

taxi.fareNote: Foreign credit/debit cards do NOT work anywhere in Iran due to sanctions — bring enough cash (US dollars or euros) to exchange into rial, or arrange a local tourist debit card. Pay taxis in cash; app rides (Snapp/Tapsi) settle in cash too unless you have an Iranian bank card.

emergency.note: 110 is police, 115 is emergency medical/ambulance, and 125 reaches the fire brigade.

solo.f: comfortable; hijab and modest dress required

avoid.reason: No no-go areas in the city itself, but avoid overland routes toward the Sistan-Baluchestan border region to the southeast.

hood_desc: The historic heart of Kerman, wrapped around the Safavid-era Ganjali Khan complex — its square, mosque, bathhouse and caravanserai — and the sprawling covered Grand Bazaar with its spice arcades, teahouses and the Jameh Mosque; best for first-time visitors who want the sights on their doorstep.

The city's central hub around Azadi (Freedom) Square, a busy roundabout where the main boulevards meet, lined with banks, shops, snack stands and taxi stops; a convenient, well-connected base for getting anywhere in town.

A modern tree-lined boulevard that is Kerman's main dining and going-out strip, packed with restaurants, fast-food joints, cafes and hotels; the liveliest street in this conservative city once the sun goes down.
A long commercial artery running off the old centre, densely packed with shops, textile and carpet dealers, gold sellers and everyday markets; the place to shop and watch daily Kermani life.

water.note: Tap is treated but bottled water is safer here.

transit.hours: Buses generally run from around 6:00 AM to about 9–10:00 PM; after that, ride-hailing apps (Snapp/Tapsi) or shared taxis fill the gap.
transit.note: Alcohol is banned nationwide, so evening life centres on teahouses and dining rather than bars. Buses and shared taxis are cheap but signage is in Persian; Snapp and Tapsi apps make getting around far easier for visitors.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or with a rechargeable local bus card tapped on board; single rides are very cheap. There is no metro, and foreign bank cards cannot be used, so carry small rial notes.

train: Kerman Railway Station — Trans-Iranian line with services to Tehran, Yazd and Bandar Abbas, plus connections toward Bam and Zahedan

airport.name: Kerman Airport (Ayatollah Hashemi Rafsanjani Airport, KER)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up a taxi fare or restaurant bill is a kind gesture but tipping is not part of the culture.

food.name: Boz ghormeh
food.desc: Kerman's signature stew: goat simmered for hours with chickpeas, whole garlic and dried mint, finished with kashk and walnut into a thick grey sauce.

places.name: Vakil Teahouse and Restaurant
places.note: Converted historic bathhouse in the bazaar; boz ghormeh is the dish visitors come for.

places.name: Hamishe Bahar Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing local dining room serving Kerman stews at everyday prices.

places.name: Sayyah Restaurant
places.note: Popular with Kerman families for full traditional menus rather than kebab alone.

food.name: Kalam polo Kermani
food.desc: Rice layered with cabbage, herbs and tiny spiced meatballs, scented with cinnamon and dried lime; the dish Kermanis name first when asked.

places.name: Vakil Teahouse and Restaurant
places.note: Atmospheric vaulted hall in the bazaar, strongest on Kerman regional plates.

places.name: Sayyah Restaurant
places.note: Reliable place to find kalam polo cooked the way it is at home.

places.name: Hamishe Bahar Restaurant
places.note: Big portions of rice dishes, busy at lunch with local office workers.

food.name: Zireh polo with lamb
food.desc: Rice steamed with the cumin the province is famous for, served under slow-braised lamb shank; simple, fragrant and unmistakably Kermani.

places.name: Vakil Teahouse and Restaurant
places.note: Cumin rice with lamb served in a restored bathhouse chamber.

places.name: Sayyah Restaurant
places.note: Dependable rice-and-lamb cooking with local spicing.

places.name: Bazaar-e Sartasari eateries
places.note: Small counters along Iran's longest covered bazaar serving the day's rice dish.

food.name: Kashk-e bademjan and kashk kadoo
food.desc: Smoky aubergine, or in the Kerman version pumpkin, mashed with fried onion, mint oil and salty whey kashk, scooped up with sangak bread.

places.name: Vakil Teahouse and Restaurant
places.note: Standard starter here, praised by visitors alongside the boz ghormeh.

places.name: Ganjali Khan Square teahouses
places.note: Courtyard teahouses in the Safavid square serve mezze-style plates with tea.

places.name: Hamishe Bahar Restaurant
places.note: Kashk dishes as a side to the main stews, generous with the bread.

food.name: Kolompeh
food.desc: Kerman's date pastry: soft dough stamped with a floral pattern, filled with spiced date paste and cardamom, baked dry so it keeps for the road.

places.name: Sweet shops in Bazaar-e Sartasari
places.note: Boxed kolompeh sold by weight; the traditional place to buy it as a gift.

places.name: Confectioners around Ganjali Khan Square
places.note: Cluster of bakeries selling kolompeh, qottab and date sweets fresh daily.

places.name: Shops by Shazdeh Garden
places.note: Stalls at the famous desert garden selling kolompeh with tea.

food.name: Kerman pistachios and pistachio sweets
food.desc: Rafsanjan pistachios, roasted with salt and lime or ground into halva and nougat; the province supplies much of Iran's crop.

places.name: Nut sellers in Bazaar-e Sartasari
places.note: Sacks of Akbari and Kalleh Ghouchi pistachios sold loose and vacuum packed.

places.name: Ganjali Khan Square shops
places.note: Handy for buying nuts and saffron sweets on the tourist circuit.

places.name: Roadside shops toward Rafsanjan
places.note: Farm-gate prices in the orchard belt west of the city.

food.name: Chai in a bazaar teahouse
food.desc: Black tea poured from a samovar into slim glasses, drunk through a lump of nabat or a date, often with a qalyan and a game of backgammon.

places.name: Vakil Teahouse
places.note: The city's best-known teahouse, set under the domes of an old hammam.

places.name: Ganjali Khan Square teahouses
places.note: Tea in a 17th-century square, the most atmospheric spot in Kerman.

places.name: Bazaar-e Sartasari tea stalls
places.note: Working tea counters where traders take their breaks.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted yoghurt drink whisked with water and dried mint, sometimes lightly carbonated; the standard cooler against Kerman's desert heat.

places.name: Sayyah Restaurant
places.note: House doogh served by the jug with rice and kebab.

places.name: Hamishe Bahar Restaurant
places.note: Chilled doogh alongside the stews, the local default drink.

places.name: Dairy stalls in Bazaar-e Sartasari
places.note: Bottled and fresh doogh sold by the bazaar's dairy sellers.

landmarks: Ganjali Khan Complex
A magnificent Safavid ensemble of square, bathhouse, mint and mosque, its frescoed hammam-turned-museum with wax figures is Kerman's showpiece attraction.
Kerman Grand Bazaar (Bazar-e Sartasari)
One of Iran's longest covered bazaars runs a full kilometre of vaulted arcades, trading carpets, copper and cumin since Safavid times.
Shazdeh Garden (Mahan)
A UNESCO-listed miracle of cascading fountains and green terraces erupting from bare desert, this Qajar prince's garden is Persia's most dramatic paradise garden.
Shah Nematollah Vali Shrine (Mahan)
The turquoise-domed shrine of the revered 15th-century Sufi poet-saint draws pilgrims to its serene courtyards and seven ancient wooden doors.
Kaluts of Shahdad (Lut Desert)
A day trip into UNESCO-listed Dasht-e Lut reveals colossal wind-carved sand castles rising from one of Earth's hottest recorded landscapes.
Rayen Citadel
A remarkably intact mud-brick fortress city rivaling fabled Bam, its medieval walls, mansions and lanes spread beneath snow-dusted Mount Hezar.
Jabalieh Dome
A mysterious octagonal stone dome of debated Sassanid or early-Islamic origin on Kerman's eastern edge, now housing a collection of historic gravestones.
Jameh Mosque of Kerman
Founded in 1349, this four-iwan Friday mosque greets worshippers with a soaring entrance portal sheathed in brilliant blue faience tilework.
Fathabad Garden
A romantically restored Qajar garden whose illuminated pavilion reflects in long pools, giving Kerman its favourite evening promenade and photo backdrop.
Moayedi Icehouse (Yakhchal)
This towering conical mud-brick dome, an ingenious ancient refrigerator, stored winter ice through scorching desert summers centuries before electricity.

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: No international trains from Kerman - the Zahedan line east toward Pakistan carries freight and the cross-border passenger service to Quetta has not run reliably for years. Kerman is the terminus of the main line from Tehran via Yazd, with overnight trains taking about 13 hours. Book through a hotel or agent, as Raja's site does not accept foreign cards.

bus.note: No scheduled international coaches. Kerman's terminal has VIP services to Yazd (about 5 hours), Shiraz (9), Bandar Abbas (7) and Tehran (14 overnight). Buy at the terminal in cash. Transport to the Kaluts desert and Rayen castle is by hired car or tour rather than public bus.

ferry.note: Kerman is inland on the edge of the Lut desert with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. The nearest boats are the Gulf ferries from Bandar Abbas to Qeshm and Kish, about seven hours south.

full.name: Bam Citadel
full.blurb: The world's largest adobe structure, a Silk Road citadel largely destroyed by a 2003 earthquake, is being rebuilt from mudbrick.

full.name: Meymand Village
full.blurb: Homes carved directly into soft rock have housed residents of this UNESCO-listed village across a documented history of centuries.
